Neonatal Meadow jumping mice enter the world at a remarkably modest body size, with field studies consistently reporting a wet weight at birth of 0.8 grams [Wwb = 0.8 grams]. These altricial newborns are entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial weeks of life, a period characterized by rapid somatic development. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the gestation period for Zapus hudsonius has been precisely measured at 19 days [tg = 19 days], a relatively short intrauterine development typical of small-bodied dipodid rodents. This brief gestation is followed by a protracted period of lactation during which the pup transitions from complete dependency to nutritional independence. The time since birth at weaning, marking the cessation of maternal milk provisioning and the onset of solid food consumption, occurs at 28 days [tx = 28 days] after birth under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. At this developmental milestone, the young have achieved a wet weight at weaning of 7.8 grams [Wwx = 7.8 grams], nearly a tenfold increase from their birth mass, reflecting the high efficiency of maternal milk transfer during the nursing phase.

Reproductive output in the Meadow jumping mouse is predominantly constrained by the short active season available in its temperate and boreal habitats, where individuals must complete breeding, juvenile growth, and pre-hibernation fattening within a limited window. Under the stable thermal conditions characteristic of laboratory rearing at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], females typically produce litters containing 5.5 pups [N_R_i = litters containing 5.5 pups] during each reproductive event. The maximum reproductive frequency in this species is approximately 2.1 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.1 litters per year], a rate that allows females to capitalize on the brief period of summer resource abundance by producing a second litter after the first cohort has been weaned. This two-part expression of fecundity, combining a moderate litter size with a relatively high annual litter frequency, is consistent with a life-history strategy favoring relatively rapid population turnover in ephemeral meadow habitats. Such a strategy necessitates that females invest heavily in lactation over successive cycles, a physiological demand that is partially offset by the substantial adult body size that supports these energetic costs prior to the onset of hibernation.

As autumn approaches and environmental temperatures decline, the Meadow jumping mouse undergoes a series of profound physiological preparations for hibernation, with body mass serving as the primary currency for winter survival. Prior to entering torpor, individuals attain an ultimate wet weight of 35 grams [Wwi = 35 grams], representing a dramatic increase from their summer foraging mass as they deposit substantial subcutaneous and visceral lipid reserves. This pre-hibernation body mass is critical for sustaining metabolic demands throughout the winter months when the animal remains in a state of profound hypothermia within subterranean nests. The capacity to nearly double body mass from the weaning weight of approximately 7.8 grams [Wwx = approximately 7.8 grams] to this pre-hibernation peak is facilitated by an intense feeding bout during late summer, during which individuals consume large quantities of seeds, berries, and arthropods. This hyperphagic phase is hormonally driven, triggered by decreasing photoperiod and temperature cues, and represents one of the most remarkable examples of seasonal mass gain among small North American mammals, enabling survival through periods of food scarcity and extreme cold.

The maturation timeline of Zapus hudsonius is tightly coupled to the brevity of the active season, with reproductive development proceeding rapidly in juveniles born early in the year. Under the controlled temperature conditions of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the time since birth at puberty for this species is 61 days [tp = 61 days], an interval that allows individuals born in spring to attain sexual maturity and potentially contribute to the second reproductive pulse of the summer. This rapid attainment of gonadal competence is an adaptive response to a short growing season; individuals that fail to mature quickly miss the opportunity to breed in their first year, a significant fitness cost in a species with relatively high annual mortality. The developmental trajectory from neonatal mass of 0.8 grams [Wwb = 0.8 grams] through weaning at 7.8 grams [Wwx = 7.8 grams] and up to the ultimate adult weight of 35 grams [Wwi = 35 grams] is characterized by an initial period of exponential growth followed by a plateau as resources are diverted toward reproductive structures. Captive-reared animals demonstrate that this pubertal transition is highly sensitive to nutritional plane, with food-restricted individuals showing substantial delays in the onset of first estrus, underscoring the energetic bottleneck imposed by the need to simultaneously grow and prepare for hibernation.

Longevity in the Meadow jumping mouse is modest compared to larger-bodied hibernators, though the species exhibits remarkable survival for a rodent of its size when considered in the context of its extreme life history. The maximum lifespan recorded in wild populations, when analyzed under the standard temperature baseline of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], is approximately 2044 days [am = approximately 2044 days], which translates to roughly 5.6 years. This comparatively extended lifespan, relative to non-hibernating rodents of similar body mass such as Peromyscus species, is likely a direct consequence of the metabolic depression associated with torpor, which effectively slows the accumulation of oxidative damage and cellular senescence over the winter months. The ultimate wet weight of 35 grams [Wwi = 35 grams] attained prior to hibernation is thus not merely a fuel reserve for winter survival but also a predictor of overwintering success and, by extension, overall lifespan, as individuals entering torpor with insufficient fat stores face elevated risks of mortality. Furthermore, the reproductive rate of 5.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5.5 pups per litter] combined with a capacity for 2.1 litters annually [F_R_i = 2.1 litters annually] ensures that despite relatively high mortality rates among juveniles and overwintering adults, populations can persist and even expand rapidly during favorable years, a demographic flexibility essential for a species inhabiting spatially and temporally variable meadow ecosystems.
